lessons.title: Lesson 1: Spotting hazards with a hazard walk
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Walk an area and list the hazards you see by type.
This lesson builds toward: During a walk through a workplace, store room or home, you will identify hazards, name the type of each, and decide whether to fix or report it, listing at least five hazards with the right type.
A hazard is anything at work that could hurt someone: a wet floor, a cord across a walkway, a heavy box on a high shelf, a machine without its guard, a leaking chemical, loud noise or a blocked exit.
A hazard walk is a slow, planned look around an area. Look down (floors, cords, spills), look up (high shelves, overhead loads, ladders), look around (machines, vehicles, chemicals, exits, fire extinguishers), and listen (loud noise, alarms, strange sounds from equipment).
Group what you find: slips, trips and falls; lifting and strains; chemicals; machines and moving parts; electrical; vehicles such as forklifts; heat, cold and noise; and fire and exits.
When you find a hazard, fix it right away if it is small and safe to do so (wipe a spill, move a box out of a walkway), then tell your supervisor. If it is not safe or you were not trained, keep people away and report it.
Step by step:
- Pick an area and walk slowly.
- Look down: floors, cords, spills.
- Look up: shelves, overhead loads, ladders.
- Look around: machines, vehicles, chemicals, exits.
- Write each hazard and its type.
- Fix small ones if safe, and report everything to your supervisor.
Words to know:
- Hazard: something at work that could cause an injury or illness.
- Hazard walk: a slow, planned walk through an area to look for hazards.
- Guard: a cover or barrier on a machine that keeps hands and bodies away from moving parts.
Try it now: Do a five-minute hazard walk in one room of your home, a store room or your workplace. Write down at least five hazards and the type of each.
You can now walk an area, spot hazards by type, and decide whether to fix or report each one.

check.q: In a hazard walk, what does "look down" mean checking?
check.why: Looking down means checking the floor for cords, spills and things you could trip on.

check.q: You find a guard missing on a machine you were not trained to fix. What do you do?
options: Keep people away and report it
check.why: If a hazard is not safe for you to fix, keep people away and report it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Using PPE the right way
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose, check and wear the right protective equipment for a task.
This lesson builds toward: Given a work task and its hazards, you will choose and check the right PPE for each hazard, matching the gear to every hazard and spotting damaged gear.
Personal protective equipment (PPE) is gear you wear to protect your body: safety glasses or goggles, face shields, hard hats, gloves, safety-toe boots, hearing protection (earplugs or earmuffs), high-visibility vests, respirators and fall-protection harnesses.
Match the gear to the hazard: glasses for flying chips or splashes; the right gloves for the job (cut-resistant for blades, chemical gloves for chemicals, as the safety data sheet says); hearing protection for loud tools; a hard hat where things can fall; a high-visibility vest near vehicles.
Check it before each use: no cracks, holes or worn straps. It must fit. A respirator must be fit-tested and you must be trained before you use one.
PPE is the last line of defense. It is better to remove a hazard first, for example by putting a guard on a machine or storing heavy items low. Under OSHA rules, employers generally must provide required PPE and train you to use it.
Step by step:
- Look at the task and its hazards.
- Pick the PPE that matches each hazard.
- Inspect it for damage.
- Put it on and check the fit.
- Clean and store it after use; report damaged gear.
Words to know:
- PPE: personal protective equipment: gear you wear to protect yourself from hazards.
- Respirator: a mask that protects your lungs from dust, fumes or gases; it needs a fit test and training.
- Fit test: a check that a respirator seals properly on your face.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Personal protective equipment
Try it now: Pick three tasks: cutting boxes with a box cutter, mopping with a cleaning chemical, and running a leaf blower. For each, write the PPE you would wear and why.
You can now choose, check and wear the right PPE for a task, and know it is the last line of defense.

check.q: What is the main reason to check PPE before each use?
options: To see if it is the newest model
To make sure the color matches
To find cracks, holes or worn straps
To count how many you have
check.why: Damaged gear may not protect you, so you check it before every use.

check.q: You will cut boxes with a box cutter all day. Which gloves do you pick?
check.why: Cut-resistant gloves match the hazard of a blade.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Slips, trips, falls and safe lifting
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Prevent slips, trips and falls and lift a load safely.
This lesson builds toward: When working on floors, ladders or with loads, you will demonstrate the steps that prevent slips, trips and falls and a safe lift, following every step without twisting your back.
Slips, trips and falls are among the most common work injuries. Prevent them: clean spills right away and put out a wet floor sign; keep walkways clear of cords, boxes and hoses; use handrails; wear shoes with good grip; and keep work areas well lit.
Working up high: use the right ladder, set it on firm, level ground, keep three points of contact (two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand), and never stand on the top step. Fall protection, such as guardrails or a harness, is required at certain heights; OSHA's general rule is 4 feet in general industry and 6 feet in construction. Follow your site's training.
Lifting: plan the lift and check the weight. Get help or use a cart, dolly or forklift for heavy or awkward loads. Stand close with feet apart, bend your knees, keep your back straight, hold the load close, lift with your legs, and turn with your feet instead of twisting your back.
Report pain early. Small strains get worse if you keep working through them.
Step by step:
- Clean spills and mark wet floors.
- Keep walkways clear.
- On a ladder: firm ground, three points of contact, not the top step.
- Before lifting: check the weight and get help or a cart if needed.
- Lift: bend knees, straight back, load close, lift with legs, turn with your feet.
Words to know:
- Three points of contact: always having two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand, on a ladder.
- Fall protection: guardrails, safety nets or harnesses that stop or prevent falls from height.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Fall protection
- OSHA: Walking-working surfaces
Try it now: Practice a safe lift with a box of books or groceries: check the weight, stand close, bend your knees, keep your back straight, lift with your legs and turn with your feet. Then write three things you would fix to stop slips and trips where you work or live.
You can now prevent slips, trips and falls, use a ladder safely, and lift a load the right way.

check.q: What should you never stand on when using a ladder?
check.why: Standing on the top step makes it easy to lose balance and fall.

check.q: You need to turn while carrying a box. How do you do it?
options: Hold the box far from your body
check.why: Turning with your feet keeps your back straight and avoids strains.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Chemicals, injuries and your rights

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Chemicals and safety data sheets
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find the hazards, PPE and first aid for a chemical on its safety data sheet.
This lesson builds toward: Given a chemical product, you will find the hazards, PPE and first aid on its label and safety data sheet, naming the right SDS sections (2, 4 and 8).
Many workplaces use hazardous chemicals: cleaners, bleach, degreasers, paint, fuel, pesticides. OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard says workers have the right to know about the chemicals they work with.
Containers must have labels showing the product name, pictograms (red-bordered symbols), a signal word ("Danger" for more serious hazards, "Warning" for less serious ones), and hazard and precaution statements.
Every hazardous chemical has a safety data sheet (SDS) with 16 sections in the same order. Useful ones: Section 2, hazards; Section 4, first aid; Section 7, safe handling and storage; Section 8, exposure controls and PPE. Your employer must keep SDSs for the chemicals you use and train you on them. Ask where they are kept.
Safe habits: never mix chemicals (bleach and ammonia make a toxic gas), keep chemicals in labeled containers, use the PPE in Section 8, and work with good air flow.
Step by step:
- Read the container label: name, pictograms, signal word.
- Find the SDS for the product.
- Section 2: what are the hazards?
- Section 8: what PPE do I need?
- Section 4: what is the first aid?
- Never mix chemicals, and keep them labeled.
Words to know:
- Safety data sheet (SDS): a 16-section document about a chemical: its hazards, safe handling, PPE and first aid.
- Pictogram: a symbol in a red diamond on a chemical label that shows the type of hazard.
- Signal word: "Danger" (more serious) or "Warning" (less serious) on a chemical label.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Hazard Communication
Try it now: Find a cleaning product at home or work. Read its label (pictograms and signal word). Then search the product name plus "safety data sheet" on the maker's website, and write down what Sections 2, 4 and 8 say.
You can now read a chemical label and find the hazards, PPE and first aid on its safety data sheet.

check.q: What is a pictogram on a chemical label?
options: A red-bordered symbol that shows a hazard
check.why: Pictograms are red-bordered symbols that show the type of hazard.

check.q: A product splashes in a coworker's eye. Which SDS section do you look at?
check.why: Section 4 of the safety data sheet gives the first aid steps.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reporting injuries and hazards
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take the right steps when someone is hurt and report it correctly.
This lesson builds toward: When someone is hurt or you find a hazard, you will list the steps to respond and write a short injury or hazard report, including what, when, where and who saw it, reported right away.
If someone is badly hurt, call 911 (or your site's emergency number) first. Do not move them unless they are in danger. Get the trained first-aider if your site has one.
Report every work injury or illness to your supervisor right away, even small ones like a cut or a strain. Early reports get you care, protect your right to workers' compensation in your state, and help fix the hazard so it does not hurt someone else. Write down what happened, when, where and who saw it.
Employers have duties too. They must report to OSHA within 8 hours if a worker dies from a work incident, and within 24 hours if a worker is admitted to a hospital as an in-patient, has an amputation or loses an eye. Many employers must also keep injury records, and workers have the right to see them.
Report hazards the same way: tell your supervisor, write it down, and keep people away until it is fixed. OSHA rules make it illegal for an employer to punish you for reporting an injury or a hazard.
Step by step:
- Serious injury: call 911 or the site emergency number first.
- Get first aid from a trained person.
- Tell your supervisor right away, even for small injuries.
- Write down what, when, where and who saw it.
- Ask about workers' compensation and follow up on the fix.
Words to know:
- Workers' compensation: state insurance that pays medical costs and some lost wages for work injuries.
- Injury log: the employer's record of work injuries and illnesses; workers have the right to see it.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Report a fatality or severe injury
- OSHA: 29 CFR 1904.39 reporting rule
Try it now: Write the steps you would take if a coworker cut their hand badly on a box cutter. Then write a short injury report: what happened, when, where, who saw it, and what should change.
You can now respond to an injury, report it correctly and on time, and know what your employer must report.

check.q: Which details belong in an injury report?
options: What happened, when, where and who saw it
Only the name of the injured worker
Who you think is to blame
check.why: A clear report says what happened, when, where and who saw it.

check.q: You strain your back lifting but it only hurts a little. What do you do?
options: Wait a month to see if it gets worse
check.why: Reporting early gets you care and protects your workers' compensation rights.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your safety rights, OSHA 10 and OSHA 30
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain your right to a safe job, how to file an OSHA complaint, and what OSHA 10 and 30 are.
This lesson builds toward: Given a safety problem that is not fixed or a job you want, you will explain your safety rights, how to file an OSHA complaint, and whether OSHA 10 or OSHA 30 fits, naming the right steps and course without help.
Under the Occupational Safety and Health Act, your employer must provide a workplace free from serious known hazards. You have the right to training in a language you understand, to required safety gear, to see injury records and test results about hazards, to report hazards, and to ask OSHA to inspect your workplace.
If a hazard is not fixed, you can file a complaint with OSHA online, by phone at 1-800-321-OSHA (6742), by mail or at an OSHA office, and ask that your name not be shared with your employer. If your employer punishes you for raising a safety concern, file a whistleblower complaint with OSHA as soon as possible; under federal law the deadline is 30 days.
OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 are courses in OSHA's voluntary Outreach Training Program. OSHA 10 is a 10-hour course for entry-level workers on hazard awareness and worker rights. OSHA 30 is a 30-hour course for supervisors and workers with safety responsibilities. There are versions for construction and for general industry. You get a course completion card.
The cards are not a license or certification, but many employers, unions and some states ask for them. Only OSHA-authorized trainers can issue real cards, so take the course from an authorized trainer or provider and be wary of offers that seem too cheap or too fast.
Step by step:
- Report a hazard to your supervisor first, if safe.
- If not fixed, file an OSHA complaint online or at 1-800-321-6742.
- Ask that your name be kept private if you want.
- If punished for reporting, file a whistleblower complaint within 30 days.
- Choose OSHA 10 (entry level) or OSHA 30 (supervisor), construction or general industry, from an authorized trainer.
Words to know:
- OSHA: the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal agency for workplace safety.
- Outreach Training Program: OSHA's voluntary program of 10-hour and 30-hour safety courses taught by authorized trainers.
- Whistleblower: a worker who reports a problem; the law protects them from being punished for it.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Workers' rights
- OSHA: File a safety and health complaint
- OSHA: Outreach Training Program
- OSHA: The facts about obtaining an OSHA card
Try it now: Final task: do a 10-minute hazard walk and write your hazard report: five hazards, their type, the PPE or fix, who you would report each to, the SDS sections for one chemical, and your injury steps. At the bottom, write whether OSHA 10 or OSHA 30 fits your job and why.
You can now explain your right to a safe job, file an OSHA complaint, and choose between OSHA 10 and OSHA 30.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Hazards found Fewer than five hazards, or types are missing or wrong. At least five hazards, each with the right type. Also says which hazards to fix now and which to report. PPE and fixes No PPE or fix, or gear that does not match the hazard. Each hazard has a PPE item or fix that matches it. Names a way to remove the hazard before relying on PPE. Safety data sheet No chemical, or the wrong SDS sections. Names Sections 2, 4 and 8 for one chemical and what each covers. Also notes the label's signal word and pictograms. Reporting No one named to report to, or injury steps missing. Names who to report each hazard to and lists the injury steps in order. The injury steps include writing what, when, where and who saw it. Rights and training Does not say whether OSHA 10 or 30 fits. Chooses OSHA 10 or OSHA 30 and gives a reason that fits their job. Also explains how to file an OSHA complaint if a hazard is not fixed. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is an OSHA 10 or OSHA 30 card?
options: A course completion card from an authorized trainer
A card that replaces employer training
check.why: The cards show you finished a voluntary outreach course; they are not a license.

check.q: You told your supervisor about a blocked fire exit and nothing changed. What can you do next?
options: File a complaint with OSHA and ask to keep your name private
check.why: If a hazard is not fixed, you can file an OSHA complaint and ask that your name not be shared.
